title: Study finds AI coding agents barely benefit from writing their own tests
key_facts: Researchers from Singapore Management University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University and ByteDance studied how AI coding agents use tests they write themselves.
They tested agents on SWE-bench Verified, a benchmark of 500 real bugs from open-source Python projects.
The number of tests an agent wrote had no statistically significant effect on whether it fixed the bug.
Agents mostly used print statements to look at values rather than assertions that pass or fail; for Claude Opus 4.5, print statements were more than 82% of feedback signals.
The paper was first posted to arXiv in February 2026 and revised in April.
The article adds its own advice that teams should rely on independent tests, which is the outlet's opinion.
quote_evidence: Across the models tested, how many tests an agent wrote during a task had no statistically significant effect on whether it actually fixed the bug.
For Claude Opus 4.5, print statements accounted for more than 82% of the feedback signals in its self-written tests.
why_it_matters_hint: Letting an AI agent grade its own work may give less reassurance than the marketing suggests.
